title: Love, and do what you will
hookLine: Augustine's line: love, then do what you want, because love will guide it

lines: LOVE, AND DO WHAT THOU WILT.
cards: "Love, and do what thou wilt." That's a bishop talking.

Augustine is preaching through the first letter of John, a short letter that keeps circling back to one word, and in the middle of a sermon he folds the whole moral life into one short command. Do what you want?
From a bishop? It sounds like a permission slip, and it can be quoted like one: to excuse a shortcut, a betrayal, a cruelty that felt honest at the time. In its place, it means something much harder.

teach.b: Look at what Augustine is talking about when he says it. Not doing whatever feels good: correction. In the same sermon he sets two scenes side by side.
A father disciplines his son, and it looks harsh. A kidnapper is gentle with a child he has stolen, and it looks kind. Which one loves?
You can't tell from the outside.
You have to look at the root: the same act can grow from love or from something else entirely. Then comes the line, and right after it, the examples. If you keep silent, keep silent out of love.
If you speak up, speak up out of love. If you correct, correct out of love. If you spare, spare out of love.
Augustine isn't inventing this. He's reading the letter in front of him: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God."

teach.h: LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.
teach.b: And Paul, writing to Rome, lists the commandments, do not kill, do not steal, and says they're all summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself: "love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law."

So the rules aren't thrown out. They're gathered up. Over the coming days the path walks through the commandments one at a time, and Augustine's line is the lens: each rule is what love looks like in one corner of life.
In his sermon, love isn't a warm mood. It wants the other person's real good, even when that costs you their approval. That makes it a stricter test than any rule, not a looser one.

how: Some Christian teachers quote Augustine's "love, and do what you will" when teaching that love of God and neighbor is the heart of the moral life, and some preachers pair it with Paul's words that love is the fulfilling of the law.

o: wanting another person's real good, even when it costs you
a warm feeling of liking someone a great deal
being agreeable so that nobody is ever upset with you

games.q: inside Augustine's line — tap the pairs.
p: preaching on the first letter of John
is gentle, and it looks kind

s: Augustine's line means anything goes, as long as it feels loving
in his sermon, the line is about correction: the same act can come from love or not, so look at the root.
Augustine was preaching on the first letter of John
a letter that says, "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God."
Paul says love does away with the commandments
he says love sums them up: "love is the fulfilling of the law."

games.q: you're a parent. your child is about to do something that will hurt them, and saying no will make them furious with you. Augustine's line is love, and do what you will. what does it ask of you?
o: say yes: love means keeping them happy.
say no, out of love, and take the anger.
say nothing: it isn't your business.
games.why: Augustine's own example is a father who disciplines his son. it looks harsh, but the root is love. if you correct, he says, correct out of love.

practice: Bring to mind one decision waiting for you, a reply you owe, a no you're dreading, a correction you might give, and ask Augustine's question: what's at the root here, love for this person, or fear, or pride, or wanting to be liked?
Don't decide yet; just look at the root, honestly. If you pray, you can hold the choice before God in silence.

wordCard.voice: Love. In Augustine's line, the root every act should grow from: wanting the other person's real good, whether that means speaking up or staying quiet.

orig.note: Greek: love. The word in 1 John 4:7, the letter Augustine was preaching on.

carryVoice: Your line: love decides. Stricter or gentler, the act follows the root. See you tomorrow.
